plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000054) on Alexey Pajitnov and Tetris: 1984 Moscow computer center, pentomino inspiration, the name, text-character graphics, spread across Moscow, state ownership of rights, and his 1996 co-founding of a company that controls the name. Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Ten items, five aimed at hard (clause logic with NO CHANGE key, specific-evidence goal, relevance, not...but punctuation, unnecessary comma). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Falling Into Place
passages.text:
[1] In 1984, Alexey Pajitnov was working as a researcher at a computer center of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. [2] In his spare time, he wrote small programs to test what the center's computers could {{1|do, one}} of them became the most famous puzzle game in the world.

[3] The idea came from pentominoes, a puzzle in which players fit together shapes made of five squares. [4] Pajitnov simplified the shapes to four squares each and set them {{2|falling, so that players had to rotate}} them quickly into place. [5] When a horizontal row was completely filled, it vanished, {{3|and so, as a result, the}} pieces above it dropped down. [6] He named the game Tetris, combining "tetra," the Greek prefix for four, with "tennis," his favorite sport.

[7] The computer Pajitnov used could not display graphics, so the first version drew {{4|it's}} pieces with letters and brackets. [8] Even so, colleagues who tried the game {{5|found it difficult to stop playing.}} [9] Copies spread from machine to machine across Moscow{{6| and}} then beyond the Soviet Union. {{7|}}

[10] Because Pajitnov had written the game at a state institution, the rights to it belonged {{8|not to him, but to the government}}. [11] For years, he earned almost nothing from it. [12] {{9|Eventually, though,}} he moved to the United States and, in 1996, co-founded a company that controls the Tetris name.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: of them became the most famous puzzle game in the world
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a period correctly separates them.

A.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

hints: Can each part stand alone as a sentence?

strategy.explanation: Test each side of the punctuation.

candidates.remember: Separate two independent clauses with a period or semicolon.

candidates.subskill: Precision and logic of a clause
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: falling, although players had to rotate
choices.C: falling, so that players having to rotate
choices.D: falling so, that players had to rotate

candidates.explanation: "So that" correctly shows the result of setting the pieces falling: players had to rotate them quickly into place.

B.rationale: "Although" signals a contrast, but rotating the pieces is the result of their falling, not a contrast with it.

C.rationale: "Having" leaves the clause after "so that" without a main verb.

D.rationale: The comma after "so" breaks up the conjunction "so that."

hints: What is the relationship between the falling pieces and the rotating?

strategy.explanation: Check the logic before the grammar.

candidates.remember: Choose the connector that shows the actual relationship.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: and as a result of this, the
choices.C: and consequently, because of this, the

candidates.explanation: "So the pieces above it dropped down" shows the result once, without repeating it.

A.rationale: "So" and "as a result" say the same thing.

B.rationale: "As a result of this" is wordy and repeats the cause-and-effect idea.

C.rationale: "Consequently" and "because of this" say the same thing.

hints: Do any words repeat an idea already clear from context?
candidates.remember: When choices mean the same thing, choose the most concise.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The pieces belong to the first version, so the possessive "its" is needed.

A.rationale: "It's" means "it is," which does not make sense before "pieces."

C.rationale: "Their" is plural, but it refers to the singular "first version."

hints: Can you replace it with "it is"?

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively shows how strongly the game appealed to the people who first tried it?

choices.B: thought it was an interesting program.
choices.C: kept playing long after they meant to get back to work.
choices.D: noticed that its pieces were drawn with letters and brackets.

candidates.explanation: Choice C describes specific behavior, playing long after meaning to return to work, which shows strong appeal.

A.rationale: "Found it difficult to stop" is general; it does not show the appeal as vividly as a specific behavior.

B.rationale: "Interesting" is mild and does not show strong appeal.

D.rationale: This describes the graphics, not the game's appeal.

hints: Which choice shows rather than tells?
candidates.remember: Specific details support a claim better than general ones.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Across Moscow and then beyond the Soviet Union" is a compound phrase, not two clauses, so no punctuation is needed before "and."

B.rationale: A comma before "and" is used to join independent clauses, but "then beyond the Soviet Union" is not a clause.

C.rationale: A semicolon cannot introduce a phrase that is not an independent clause.

D.rationale: This would leave "And then beyond the Soviet Union" as a fragment.

hints: Is the part after "and" a complete clause?

strategy.explanation: Check whether "then beyond the Soviet Union" has a subject and verb.

candidates.remember: Do not put a comma before "and" when it joins two phrases.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Some researchers have studied whether puzzle games improve spatial reasoning.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the game spread so quickly across Moscow.
choices.B: Yes, because it supports the claim that colleagues found the game hard to stop.
choices.C: No, because it contradicts the claim that the game was simple.
choices.D: No, because it shifts from the game's spread to a separate research question.

candidates.evidence: Copies spread from machine to machine across Moscow
candidates.explanation: The paragraph describes the early version and the game's spread; a sentence about research on spatial reasoning interrupts that focus.

A.rationale: The sentence does not explain the game's spread; it raises an unrelated question about effects.

B.rationale: The sentence concerns research on reasoning, not why people kept playing.

C.rationale: The sentence does not address whether the game was simple.

strategy.explanation: Compare the sentence with the paragraph's focus.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it develops the paragraph's point.

candidates.subskill: Unnecessary comma in a "not ... but" construction
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: not to him but to the government
choices.C: not to him; but to the government
choices.D: not, to him but, to the government

candidates.explanation: "Not to him but to the government" is one paired construction, so no comma is needed between its parts.

A.rationale: A comma should not separate the paired parts of "not ... but."

C.rationale: A semicolon cannot join two phrases.

D.rationale: These commas break up the phrases for no reason.

hints: Are the two parts joined by "but" clauses or phrases?
candidates.remember: Don't separate correlative pairs with commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: he earned almost nothing from it
candidates.explanation: Sentence 12 describes a later change that contrasts with sentence 11, so "Eventually, though," fits.

B.rationale: Moving to the United States is not an example of earning nothing.

C.rationale: Earning nothing did not cause him to co-found a company years later.

D.rationale: Co-founding a company that controls the name contrasts with earning nothing; it is not similar.

hints: How does sentence 12 relate to sentence 11?
candidates.remember: Use a contrast transition when a situation changes.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how a popular game was created and how its creator came to profit from it. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains in detail how the game earned money in the Soviet Union.
choices.B: No, because it focuses mainly on the history of the pentomino puzzle.
choices.C: Yes, because it traces the game's creation and Pajitnov's later stake in its name.
choices.D: No, because it says that Pajitnov never earned anything from the game.

candidates.evidence: co-founded a company that controls the Tetris name
candidates.explanation: The essay describes how Pajitnov created the game and how, after years of earning almost nothing, he co-founded a company that controls the name.

A.rationale: The essay says Pajitnov earned almost nothing for years; it does not explain Soviet earnings.

B.rationale: Pentominoes are mentioned only as the game's inspiration.

D.rationale: The essay says he earned almost nothing "for years," then co-founded a company that controls the name.

hints: Does the essay cover both the creation and the profit?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against both parts of the purpose.

candidates.remember: A purpose with two parts requires both to be met.
